Amino acids are organic molecules that serve as the building blocks of proteins. Each amino acid contains an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a distinctive side chain, all bonded to a central carbon atom. Twenty standard amino acids are incorporated into proteins during translation, and their diverse chemical properties ranging from hydrophobic to polar to charged determine the structure and function of the resulting protein.

Every amino acid has the same backbone: an amino group, a carboxyl group, and a hydrogen atom, all bonded to a central alpha carbon. The side chain attached to this alpha carbon distinguishes one amino acid from another and determines its chemical properties. Amino acids link together via peptide bonds. The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, releasing a water molecule and forming a carbon-nitrogen bond. The resulting polymer is a polypeptide or protein, and the order of amino acids in this sequence is crucial because it determines the protein's function.

The twenty standard amino acids fall into several categories based on their properties. The hydrophobic or nonpolar amino acids include alanine, valine, leucine, and isoleucine, which are small to medium-sized and used to form hydrophobic cores in protein interiors. There's also phenylalanine, tryptophan, and proline. Phenylalanine and tryptophan are aromatic and can absorb ultraviolet light. Proline is special because it restricts the backbone's conformation. Methionine contains sulfur and is also the start amino acid.

The polar uncharged amino acids include serine, threonine, and cysteine, which contain hydroxyl or thiol groups and are involved in hydrogen bonding and often sites of post-translational modification. Asparagine and glutamine have amide side chains and are polar and involved in hydrogen bonding. Glycine is unique because it has only a hydrogen as its side chain, making it the smallest amino acid and offering flexibility in tight turns and loops.

The charged positive amino acids are lysine, arginine, and histidine. Lysine and arginine are basic amino acids that are positively charged at physiological pH and involved in salt bridges and DNA or RNA binding. Histidine is weakly basic and can be protonated or deprotonated near physiological pH, making it important in enzyme active sites and metal coordination.

The charged negative amino acids are aspartate and glutamate, which are acidic amino acids negatively charged at physiological pH. They're involved in salt bridges and often found on protein surfaces.

The genetic code specifies which amino acid should be incorporated at each position. Sixty-four codons encode the twenty amino acids, a system called the degenerate code. Transfer RNA molecules are charged with amino acids by enzymes called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and recognizes the appropriate codon. Amino acids have another important property called chirality. Amino acids except glycine have a chiral center at the alpha carbon. Proteins use only left-handed amino acids, while bacteria and some other organisms use right-handed amino acids in their cell walls.

About twenty additional amino acids occur in proteins through post-translational modification, including hydroxyproline found in collagen and hydroxylysine. Some organisms and engineered systems incorporate selenocysteine and pyrrolysine as the twenty-first and twenty-second amino acids, expanding the genetic code.

Amino acids are essential to biochemistry. The discovery that proteins are built from a standard set of amino acids, and that the genetic code specifies which amino acid goes where, unified molecular biology in the nineteen sixties. The diversity of the twenty amino acids allows cells to construct proteins with astonishing variety: rigid structural proteins, flexible fibrous proteins, globular enzymes with exquisite specificity. Understanding amino acids is essential to molecular biology and medicine.
